candidate.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity → Mental Health Concepts/Coping: recognize signs and symptoms of depression, assess alterations in mood and coping, provide psychosocial support, and facilitate referral when mental-health needs affect client functioning or care.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — depression as a barrier to self-care in chronic heart failure
candidate.educational_objective: Recognize depression as a clinically important psychosocial barrier to heart-failure self-care and assess/refer appropriately without attributing physical heart-failure symptoms to a mental-health diagnosis alone.

options.A: Depression can interfere with heart-failure self-care and is associated with poorer clinical and quality-of-life outcomes, so recognizing it can guide appropriate psychosocial support and referral.
options.B: Depressive symptoms are expected in heart failure and generally should not be assessed unless the client requests psychiatric hospitalization.
options.C: Mental-health symptoms have little relationship to heart-failure self-care, so screening would not affect the nursing plan.
options.D: A positive depression screen would prove that the client's fatigue and reduced activity are entirely psychiatric rather than potentially related to heart failure.

candidate.rationale: The AHA/ACC/HFSA heart-failure guideline identifies depression as a barrier to effective heart-failure self-care and notes associations with poor self-care, rehospitalization, mortality, and impaired quality of life. The guideline includes validated depression screening tools among examples for identifying barriers and supports multidisciplinary mental-health and social support when needed. A positive screen does not by itself establish that physical symptoms are psychiatric or replace broader clinical assessment. Therefore, A is correct; B and C minimize an important comorbidity, and D creates false diagnostic certainty.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Directly supports depression assessment as relevant to heart-failure self-care and outcomes and supports multidisciplinary psychosocial evaluation rather than dismissing symptoms or attributing all physical symptoms to depression.
candidate.source_document_title: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure
candidate.source_locator: Section 7.1.1, Self-Care Support in HF → Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text 4: depression is a risk factor for poor HF self-care, rehospitalization, and all-cause mortality. Table 11, Potential Barriers to Effective HF Self-Care and Example Interventions: depression is a medical barrier; example screening tools include HAM-D, BDI-II and PHQ-9, with psychotherapy, SSRI treatment, and nurse-led support listed as possible interventions. Section 10.1 notes depression is common in HF and strongly affects quality of life and outcomes, while conventional antidepressant therapy has not consistently improved HF outcomes.
candidate.source_organization: American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology/Heart Failure Society of America
candidate.stem: A client with chronic heart failure reports persistent sadness, loss of interest, and increasing difficulty following the self-care plan. Why should the nurse assess the client further for depression?
